text: You've cracked open hundreds of these, and not one of them was Chinese.
An eighteen seventy-eight print from Kyoto shows a baker grilling these exact cookies.
Bigger, darker, made with sesame and miso, with the fortune tucked into the fold.
Japanese bakers brought them to California.
A tea garden in San Francisco served them with green tea, and a family bakery made them by the thousands.
Then, in nineteen forty-two, Japanese Americans on the West Coast were sent to internment camps, and the bakeries closed.
More than a hundred thousand people lost their homes and their businesses.
Chinese American factories filled the gap, and put a cookie at the end of every Chinese meal.
Today, about three billion are made every year.
One factory in New York makes more than four million of them a day.
And when a company tried selling them in China, they flopped. Why? They were too American.
So the most Chinese thing on your table was Japanese all along.
Did you learn something new? Like, and subscribe.
